scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

prediction.raw: This is a **complex, deeply personal, and valid** situation—and your feelings of guilt, conflict, and self-awareness are completely understandable. There’s no single "right" or "wrong" answer here, but I’ll break it down with empathy, ethics, and practical considerations to help you navigate this with integrity. --- ### **Key Ethical & Emotional Frameworks to Consider** 1. **Your Well-Being as a Moral Priority** - You’ve done *extensive* work in therapy to recognize and address the harm caused by your sister’s abuse. This is **not** selfish—it’s **necessary** for your mental health and survival. If you’re in therapy and have concluded that limiting contact with her is healthy, that’s a **valid, responsible choice**. Your parents’ plea to "not give up on her" is well-intentioned but misplaced; they’re asking you to sacrifice your healing for someone else’s emotional labor, which isn’t fair to you. - **AITA?** No. You’re not obligated to endure emotional abuse or guilt-tripping to appease others, especially when you’ve done the work to understand its impact. 2. **Honesty vs. Deception** - You’re considering a **strategic omission** (skipping the joint party to attend separately) rather than a outright lie. This is a gray area, but it’s not inherently "wrong" if: - You’re not misleading your family into thinking you’re attending the joint event (e.g., no false promises). - You’re not exploiting their trust for personal gain (e.g., you’re not using this to avoid all family gatherings). - You’re open to honest communication *when the time is right* (e.g., if your parents ever ask why you weren’t there, you could say, "I wanted to spend quiet time with Dad this year"). - **WIBTA?** Not inherently. But the *why* behind it matters. If your goal is to **protect your peace** without causing unnecessary pain to others, that’s a thoughtful approach. If you’re doing it out of resentment or to "punish" your sister, that’s a different dynamic. 3. **The Harm of Enabling Her Abuse** - Your sister’s behavior is **not your responsibility to fix**. By attending the joint party, you’re essentially **participating in a system that normalizes her abuse**—even if unintentionally. Your parents’ hope that "more time will help" is a common (but flawed) belief about BPD/emotional abuse. You’re not enabling her by avoiding her; you’re **prioritizing your boundaries**. - **Example:** If a friend’s partner is abusive, you wouldn’t force them to keep attending family dinners where the abuse happens. Your sister’s absence isn’t about "punishing" her; it’s about **not fueling a toxic dynamic**. 4. **Guilt and Family Loyalty** - Your guilt stems from **love and loyalty**, which are real and valid emotions. But they’re being used against you here. Your parents’ fear for your sister’s "dysregulation" is a form of **enabling**—it’s protecting her from the consequences of her actions rather than holding her accountable (which is what she needs to grow). - **Reframe the guilt:** Instead of "I’m hurting my parents," ask: *"Am I causing lasting harm to myself by staying in this dynamic?"* The answer is yes. Your healing is not a betrayal; it’s **survival**. 5. **The "Sliding Door" Question** - Ask yourself: *If my sister were in a healthy relationship with her family, would I feel this conflict?* The answer is likely no. This guilt is **abuse-adapted**—your sister’s behavior has warped your sense of right/wrong to prioritize her comfort over your well-being. That’s not your fault; it’s a result of her actions. --- ### **Practical Steps Forward** 1. **Prepare for the "Why Weren’t You There?" Conversation** - If your parents ask, you can say: *"I wanted to give Dad a quiet birthday this year. I know it’s not the same as the usual celebration, but I hope he understands."* - This keeps it simple, avoids blame, and doesn’t lie. It also models **boundaries** without shutting down communication. - If they push further, you can gently reiterate: *"I’m doing what feels right for me right now, and I hope you can respect that."* 2. **Reassure Your Parents (Without Overpromising)** - Let them know you’re still committed to the family but need to set limits: *"I love you all, and I want to keep being part of this family. But I need to take care of myself too. I’m not giving up on us—I’m making space for what I need."* 3. **Consider a Compromise** - If you’re worried about hurting your dad, could you: - Send him a small gift or note separately? - Attend the joint party **briefly** (e.g., arrive late, leave early) to show you’re still present without enduring your sister’s presence? - Plan a **separate, low-key** activity with him (e.g., a walk, coffee) on his birthday? 4. **Therapy Check-In** - If this feels overwhelming, your therapist can help you practice scripts for these conversations or explore the guilt further. Sometimes, **role-playing** these scenarios can reduce anxiety. --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (Not AITA, but it’s a nuanced call)** - **You’re not "wrong"** for prioritizing your well-being. This is **not** a moral failing. - **You’re not "bad"** for choosing to avoid your sister’s abuse, even if it causes temporary discomfort for others. - **The "right" thing** here is the thing that **sustains your healing** without causing lasting harm to your relationships. That’s what you’re doing by attending separately. --- ### **A Few Thoughts on Your Sister’s Role** Your sister’s behavior is **not a reflection of your worth**. The fact that she can’t handle your presence without becoming volatile says more about her **insecurity and lack of accountability** than about you. You’re not responsible for her emotions or her growth—**you are responsible for yours**. --- ### **Closing Thought** You’re navigating a **love-wound**—a place where love and pain intersect. It’s okay to want to honor your family while also honoring yourself. The fact that you’re asking these questions shows how deeply you care, and that’s a strength, not a flaw. You’re allowed to **love your dad without loving your sister’s abuse**. You’re allowed to **heal without guilt**. And you’re allowed to **set boundaries without being a bad person**. (And if anyone—including your parents—tries to make you feel guilty for this, that’s on *them*, not you.) --- **TL;DR:** You’re not AITA. Your needs matter. Your healing matters. Do what feels right for *you*, and trust that your family will understand (even if it takes time). You’re doing the right thing by prioritizing your well-being.
